items.headline: Cushioned Shoes Still Need Structural Support
items.background: There's a persistent assumption in footwear design that high cushioning is sufficient for foot support, leading brands to deprioritize structural chassis elements in soft-soled shoes. VUZUGU-CORE™ appears to be a midsole or support technology challenging that tradeoff.
keyFindings: Cushioning and structural support address different biomechanical needs and cannot substitute for each other
VUZUGU-CORE™ is positioned as a chassis system designed to work alongside cushioning layers
The piece acknowledges the technology is unproven and still requires real-world testing
items.implications: Relevant mostly to product designers or researchers in wearables and physical product UX — this is a vendor-adjacent piece with limited independent validation. Treat claims skeptically until third-party testing exists.

items.headline: Two Design Students Map Advocacy Program Experience
items.background: Design students entering policy or civic advocacy spaces often lack frameworks for understanding those environments, and journey mapping is rarely applied to the participants' own experience rather than end users.
keyFindings: Authors used journey mapping as a reflective tool for their own participation in the YLAC Mobility Champions 2026 program
The piece documents how design thinking methods transfer — and strain — in non-commercial advocacy contexts
Co-authorship between two students suggests the reflection captures divergent as well as shared perspectives
items.implications: Useful for educators and early-career designers interested in civic design or applying UX methods in non-product contexts. Limited generalizability given the personal scope, but the reflexive use of journey mapping is a transferable technique.

items.headline: Laser-Cut Phone Stand as Critical Design Exercise
items.background: Critical design uses provocative objects to challenge assumptions about behavior and technology dependence. This student project frames a physical phone stand as a commentary on screen addiction using deliberately confrontational framing.
keyFindings: The stand is constructed from 4mm MDF using laser cutting, framed metaphorically as a 'jail cell' for the phone
The project is presented as a design reflection rather than a commercial or functional prototype
Critical design framing is used to prompt questions about phone dependency rather than solve a usability problem
items.implications: Primarily relevant to design educators and students exploring critical or speculative design methods. Not directly applicable to product or UX practice but illustrates how material choices and framing can carry conceptual weight.

items.headline: Six Habits That Took One Designer to Head of Product
items.background: The designer-to-product-leader career path is common but poorly documented in terms of which specific practices actually drive the transition versus which are retrospective rationalization.
keyFindings: The author credits a set of Figma-rooted design habits as foundational to reaching a Head of Product role
Six specific practices are identified as ones the author would repeat — implying others were abandoned or revised
The piece is first-person and retrospective, drawing from a single career trajectory rather than comparative data
items.implications: Useful for mid-career designers considering a move into product leadership, but treat as one data point. The habits described may be highly context-dependent — company size, industry, and team structure all affect which design-to-product transitions look like.

items.headline: Eight Concrete Upgrades Hasselblad's 907x CFV 100C Needs
items.background: The Hasselblad 907x CFV 100C is a high-end medium format digital back with a retro modular form factor. Despite its premium positioning, users and reviewers have identified persistent usability and feature gaps that Hasselblad has not addressed.
keyFindings: Eight specific hardware or software improvements are proposed for the 907x CFV 100C system
The critique targets a camera priced in the upper tier of the medium format market, where usability gaps are harder to justify
The piece comes from PetaPixel, a specialist photography publication with a technically literate readership
items.implications: Relevant to UX practitioners working on hardware products or camera software — illustrates how premium pricing raises usability expectations and how modular legacy form factors create interface debt.

items.headline: 74 Real Product Failures That Hurt Usability
items.background: Bad design in physical and digital products is often discussed abstractly. Compiled examples of real-world failures provide concrete evidence of how design decisions cause friction, confusion, or harm for actual users.
keyFindings: 74 documented product design failures are presented, each making tasks harder for intended users
Examples span physical and likely digital products, illustrating that poor usability is not domain-specific
The volume and specificity of examples make this a practical reference for identifying common failure patterns
items.implications: Useful as a teaching resource or heuristic reference for designers conducting design reviews or building failure-mode awareness. The AOL sourcing suggests a listicle format — useful for examples but unlikely to include structured analysis.

items.headline: Award-Winning Strength App Shows Niche Fitness UX Can Compete
items.background: The A' Design Award covers a broad range of product and interface design categories. Winning entries in app design — especially in crowded verticals like fitness — offer a benchmark for what judges and by extension users respond to.
keyFindings: HERCS, a strength-training app designed by Luhan Rong, won an A' Design Award in its category
The app targets strength training specifically, a more focused niche than general fitness apps like MyFitnessPal or Apple Fitness+
Recognition at a formal design award suggests the interface achieved distinction in visual design, usability, or innovation criteria
items.implications: Worth examining the HERCS interface directly if you work on fitness, health, or activity-tracking products — award-winning niche apps often demonstrate interaction patterns that larger competitors overlook. The A' Award is credible but broad, so weight accordingly.
